data.title: Project Brief: Migrate Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Goals
Centralize and streamline team knowledge management by migrating the current wiki platform to PlexiiWrite.
Improve content accessibility, searchability, and collaboration through a more intuitive, real-time editing environment.
Reduce technical debt associated with maintaining legacy wiki infrastructure.
Enable seamless access to documentation across all team locations, including remote and hybrid work setups.
Scope
Full migration of all existing wiki pages, including project documentation, process guides, and operational procedures.
Integration of user permissions and role-based access controls to preserve current security settings.
Onboarding of team members to use PlexiiWrite with training materials and support resources.
Migration of linked assets (e.g., images, files) where feasible; external links will remain unchanged.
Excludes third-party integrations not currently supported by PlexiiWrite (e.g., Jira, Slack).
Timeline
Week 1–2
: Finalize content inventory, define migration plan, and set up PlexiiWrite environment.
Week 3–4
: Begin phased content migration; validate accuracy and formatting.
Week 5
: Conduct internal testing and user feedback session.
Week 6
: Full go-live with live access to updated wiki.
Week 7–8
: Monitor usage, address issues, and refine workflows.
Risks
Data loss or formatting errors during migration: Mitigation through staged testing and version control.
User resistance due to unfamiliarity with new interface: Mitigation via targeted training and early access groups.
Delayed integration with existing tools: Mitigation by aligning with platform release schedules and using API-first design.
Performance issues under high concurrent access: Mitigation through load testing and proactive monitoring.
This project will ensure our team has a modern, scalable, and user-friendly knowledge base that supports ongoing collaboration and growth.

data.title: Onboarding Guide for New Support Agents – First Week

content.text: Welcome and Orientation

Welcome to the support team! This guide is designed to help you successfully integrate into our operations during your first week. You’ll gain familiarity with key tools, processes, and escalation procedures that ensure consistent, efficient, and customer-focused service.

Your first week will focus on understanding our workflows, learning how to use essential tools, and becoming comfortable with our escalation protocols. By the end of the week, you will be able to handle routine inquiries independently and know when and how to escalate more complex issues.
Day 1: Introduction and Team Overview
Attend your welcome session with the Support Operations Manager and your assigned mentor.
Review the company’s mission, values, and support team structure.
Meet your team members and learn about their roles and responsibilities.
Receive a copy of the Support Handbook and access to internal knowledge resources.
Complete the onboarding checklist and sign in to your account portal.
Note:
Your mentor will be available for questions throughout the week and will help you navigate daily tasks.
Day 2–3: Tool Familiarization
Learn how to use the core tools that support daily operations:
1. Customer Support Portal (CSAT)
Log in using your credentials.
Navigate ticket creation, viewing, and updating.
Understand the ticket lifecycle: new, in progress, resolved, closed.
Learn to apply tags, categorize issues, and assign tickets to appropriate queues.
2. CRM System (Salesforce or equivalent)
Access customer profiles and interaction history.
View past support conversations and resolution notes.
Update customer records with new information or outcomes.
3. Internal Knowledge Base
Search for standard solutions to common issues.
Bookmark frequently used articles and troubleshooting guides.
Report outdated or missing content to the Knowledge Team.
4. Communication Tools
Use Slack for team messaging, alerts, and urgent updates.
Understand channel structure (e.g., #general, #support-queue, #escalations).
Learn how to use voice and video tools for complex issue walkthroughs.
Tip:
Spend 15 minutes each day practicing ticket creation and CRM updates using sample cases from the knowledge base.
Day 4: Handling Routine Tickets
Practice handling typical support requests under supervision:
Follow the standard response template for common issues (e.g., login problems, account setup).
Use empathy-driven language in all customer interactions.
Document resolution steps clearly in the ticket system.
Confirm customer understanding before closing a ticket.
Your mentor will review your work and provide feedback on clarity, tone, and efficiency.
Day 5: Escalation Procedures
Understand when and how to escalate tickets to higher-level teams.
When to Escalate
Escalate if:
The issue is outside known solutions or requires product expertise.
Customer expresses frustration or emotional distress.
A technical or system failure is suspected and cannot be resolved within standard timeframes.
The issue involves billing, security, or compliance concerns.
Escalation Process
Identify the need for escalation
using the escalation checklist in the Support Handbook.
Add an escalation tag
(e.g., “[quote]”) to the ticket in the support portal.
Notify your supervisor or escalation lead
via Slack with:
Ticket number
Summary of issue
Customer context (name, account, recent activity)
Timeframe for resolution
Document all steps taken
before escalation.
Follow up
after resolution to ensure customer satisfaction and update the ticket closure notes.
Escalation Response Timeline
All escalations must be acknowledged within 10 minutes of being submitted.
The escalation team will respond within 15 minutes of receiving the request.
A follow-up from the agent is required within 2 hours post-resolution.
Final Steps and Next Steps
At the end of your first week:
Complete the weekly onboarding assessment (available in the portal).
Submit a short reflection on your experience and one area you’d like to improve.
Schedule a brief check-in with your mentor for feedback and next steps.
Next week, you’ll begin handling tickets independently with full support oversight. You will also attend a training session on advanced troubleshooting and customer empathy techniques.
Stay proactive, ask questions, and remember: every interaction is an opportunity to build trust and improve our service quality.
This guide was last updated on [date]. For updates or clarifications, contact the Support Operations Manager.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: Why Bug Reports Matter
bullets: Clear bug reports help developers fix issues faster
They reduce miscommunication and avoid rework
A well-written report saves time and improves team efficiency
Every bug is a chance to improve product quality
Good reports build trust between testers and developers
Consistent reporting enables better tracking and analysis
slides.notes: Start by emphasizing that bug reports are not just about finding errors—they're tools for collaboration. A clear, structured report helps everyone understand the problem and act quickly. This sets the foundation for effective teamwork.

slides.title: The Core Elements of a Good Report
bullets: Describe what happens (steps to reproduce)
State exactly what is expected vs. what actually occurs
Include environment details: device, OS, version
Add screenshots or logs if available
Specify severity level: critical, high, medium, low
Keep language simple and objective
slides.notes: Every good report must have these key components. Focus on clarity and precision—avoid assumptions or emotional language. The goal is to give developers enough information to reproduce and fix the issue without guesswork.

slides.title: How to Reproduce the Issue
bullets: Start with a clear step-by-step sequence
Use numbered steps for readability
Ensure each step is actionable and repeatable
Include any prerequisites or user actions before starting
Verify that the steps lead directly to the bug
Test with different users or devices if needed
slides.notes: Reproducibility is critical. A tester should be able to follow the steps exactly and see the same result. This helps developers validate the issue without needing extra context or assumptions.

slides.title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls
bullets: Never say 'it just broke'—be specific
Skip vague descriptions like 'something is wrong'
Don’t assume the developer knows the product flow
Avoid blaming or emotional language
Don’t include irrelevant details or personal opinions
Always verify the bug is not a user error
slides.notes: Common mistakes can waste hours of developer time. Always focus on facts, not feelings. A neutral tone and clear facts ensure the report is actionable and respectful to the engineering team.

slides.title: Example: From Vague to Clear
bullets: Vague: 'The app crashes sometimes'
Clear: 'After tapping 'Save' on profile page, app crashes on Android 12 with version 3.2.1'
Vague: 'It doesn’t work well'
Clear: 'When user submits form without required fields, error message appears but is missing field validation'
slides.notes: Show a before-and-after example to illustrate how clarity transforms a report. This makes it tangible—team members can see the difference between confusion and precision.

slides.title: Next Steps & Best Practices
bullets: Always verify the bug is reproducible before reporting
Use templates to ensure consistency across reports
Review reports with a peer for clarity and completeness
Update reports as new information emerges
Close the ticket only after fix is verified and tested
Encourage team-wide ownership of quality feedback
slides.notes: Wrap up by reinforcing daily habits: use templates, double-check details, and collaborate. A culture of clear communication leads to faster fixes and stronger team performance.

results.text:
# Performance and Memory Analysis — Widgets and Browsers

Grounded in the current code. Numbers are engineering estimates from the architecture, not measured profiles; the last section says how to measure them for real. The headline: browsers dominate memory, the canvas has no offscreen culling, and live wires are the main CPU hot path during interaction.

## 1. The model that decides everything

Three architectural facts drive every number below.

Only the active desk is mounted. `loadForTask` wipes the widget store and loads just the open task's widgets, so widgets on other desks cost nothing while you are not on them. Portals are the exception and they are cheap (see below). So "how many widgets hurt" is really "how many on ONE desk."

No viewport culling. `Canvas.tsx` renders `widgets.map((w) => renderWidget(w))` with no check for whether a widget is in view. Every widget on the active desk is fully mounted and live whether it is on screen, panned far away, or hidden behind another widget. Section children render too. There is no virtualization.

Each browser is a real Chromium process that never sleeps. `webviewTag: true`, `sandbox: false`, each `<webview>` gets its own session partition, and there is no `backgroundThrottling`, no `visibilitychange` handling, and no IntersectionObserver in `WebViewWidget`. So an offscreen or hidden browser still runs its timers, animations, video, and JavaScript at full cost. This is the single biggest stability lever in the app.

## 2. Per-widget cost

Memory is per live widget on the active desk. CPU-at-rest is the steady cost when you are not touching it.

| Widget | Est. RAM each | CPU at rest | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| webview (browser) | 80 MB light page, 150-400 MB for SPAs (Gmail, Notion, Figma, image-heavy marketing) | Medium-High; full when offscreen | Separate Chromium renderer process + the live page. No throttling. |
| local-app-launcher (mirror mode) | Native app + a capture/composite cost | Medium | Punch-through of a real native window. |
| diagram | 10-30 MB | Low-Medium | React Flow (`@xyflow/react`) is a heavy graph runtime. |
| page / markdown | 5-15 MB | Low | Full Tiptap / ProseMirror editor instance each. |
| scratchpad | 5-20 MB (grows with strokes) | Low | Canvas + perfect-freehand stroke buffers. |
| streamdeck | 3-8 MB | Low | 10x3 button grid + media/app bindings. |
| table | 2-10 MB (rows) | Low | Rows + per-cell field editors. |
| mindmap | 2-8 MB | Low | Node tree + SVG. |
| voice-recorder | small idle, large while recording | High while recording | MediaRecorder + audio buffers. |
| video / image / file | size of the media | Low-Medium | Decoded media in memory; video keeps decoding. |
| agent | 1-3 MB | Low; spikes on run | Config + run log; AI cost on each run, browser-driving cost if wired to a browser. |
| portal | 1-2 MB | Low (4s poll) | Renders a static `DeskMiniature` of another desk from a `listByTask` poll every 4s. It does NOT mount that desk's live webviews, so a control room of portals is cheap. |
| minimap | small RAM, notable CPU on re-render | Medium on change | Auto-created per desk; renders EVERY widget as a scaled live `WidgetPreview` in a foreignObject, so its re-render cost scales with widget count. |
| sticky / note / card / shape / field / calculator / color / timer / task-link | 0.2-1 MB | Negligible | DOM + React only. |

Baseline before any widgets: the main process, the GPU process, and the React renderer window together are roughly 250-450 MB.

## 3. The CPU hot paths (scale with count, not just memory)

Live wires overlay. `LinkOverlay` rebuilds its segments by calling `getBoundingClientRect` (via `querySelector` on `data-widget-id`) for BOTH endpoints of EVERY wire on every render, and it runs a `requestAnimationFrame` loop that re-renders every frame while the mouse is held. So during a drag the cost is O(wires) DOM reads per frame. With a few wires this is invisible; with 30-50+ wires and an active drag it starts dropping frames. Firing wires add SMIL animations on top, which are cheap individually but add up.

Minimap re-render. The minimap subscribes to widget/pan/zoom/layout changes and re-renders every widget as a live preview. On a desk with many widgets, every layout change re-runs that whole render. It is the second hot path after wires.

No culling means mount cost is total, not visible. Panning a huge desk keeps all editors, canvases, and especially browsers alive and compositing. The compositor has to manage every webview layer even when off screen, which is where pan/zoom jank comes from on browser-heavy desks.

Background timers (app-wide, independent of widget count): body-double presence ~30s, time-of-day tint ~1 min, plus the inbox poller, drift detector, hyperfocus guardian, focus-session ticker, and the sync indicator. None are per-widget; together they are a small, constant background load. Per-widget timers exist for interval-trigger agents and the 4s portal poll.

## 4. Risk thresholds

Browsers on one desk:
- 1-3: comfortable. Roughly 0.5-1.2 GB total. Fine everywhere.
- 4-8: 1.2-3 GB. Fine on 16 GB Macs; noticeable on 8 GB, some swap.
- 9-15: 3-6 GB, real swap pressure on 8-16 GB machines, pan/zoom jank as the compositor juggles many webview layers. Heavy SPAs (Gmail, Figma, Notion) hit the top of this range fast.
- 16+: high risk. Multi-GB swap, beachballs, and on lower-RAM machines the OS can start killing renderer processes (a browser widget goes blank). This is the most likely path to instability today.

Non-browser widgets on one desk:
- up to ~30: no perceptible cost.
- 30-60: fine at rest; drag/pan with many wires begins to show frame drops, and minimap re-renders get heavier.
- 60-120: input latency on pan/drag becomes noticeable, especially with editors (page/markdown), a diagram, or 40+ wires in play.
- 120+: sluggish even at rest from React reconciliation and the no-cull mount cost; this is well beyond normal use but reachable on a "dump everything" desk.

Wires specifically: under ~20 are free; 30-50 start to matter during drag; 80+ make dragging visibly choppy because of the per-frame O(wires) bound reads.

Live agents: not a memory cliff but a CPU and cost one. Several interval agents, or an agent driving a browser in a tool loop, add steady CPU and real API spend. The risk is runaway cost and a busy browser, not RAM.

## 5. Stability risks, ranked

1. Browser-process memory exhaustion. The clearest failure mode. Many webviews, especially heavy SPAs, can exhaust RAM and trigger OS-level renderer kills (blank browser widgets) or heavy swap. No suspension of offscreen browsers makes this worse than it needs to be.
2. Compositor jank on browser-heavy desks. Even within memory limits, many live webview layers make pan/zoom stutter because nothing is culled.
3. Drag-time wire cost. O(wires) bound reads per animation frame during drags on wire-dense desks.
4. Agent browser-driving and intervals. CPU and API cost, plus an agent navigating a shared browser the user is also using.
5. Minimap re-render cost on very dense desks.

## 6. Recommendations, prioritized

The first two remove most of the risk for the least work.

P1. Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers. Add an IntersectionObserver (or a pan/zoom-driven visibility check) in `WebViewWidget`; when a browser is fully off screen or fully occluded, stop it doing work: mute audio, and ideally detach or freeze it. Electron can `webContents.setBackgroundThrottling`, and a stronger move is to unload the `<webview>` when far offscreen and reload its URL when it returns. This directly attacks risk 1 and 2.

P2. Viewport-cull the canvas. In `Canvas.tsx`, skip mounting widgets whose bounds are well outside the viewport (with a margin), so a giant desk only mounts what is near view. Browsers benefit most. This attacks risk 2 and 5 and the no-cull mount cost generally.

P3. Soft-cap and warn on browsers per desk. Track live webview count and, past a threshold (say 8), surface a gentle "this desk has many browsers, performance may drop" hint rather than a hard limit. Cheap, prevents the worst surprises.

P4. Throttle the wire overlay. Cap the `LinkOverlay` rAF to ~30fps during drag, cache bound reads within a frame, and skip wires whose endpoints are offscreen.

P5. Throttle the minimap. Debounce its re-render and render simple rectangles instead of full `WidgetPreview` previews above a widget-count threshold.

P6. Lazy-mount heavy widgets. Defer mounting Tiptap/React Flow/scratchpad until the widget is near the viewport (a lighter version of P2 scoped to editors).

P7. A dev performance overlay. Surface `app.getAppMetrics()` (per-process memory and CPU) and a live widget/webview/wire count so this analysis can be replaced with real numbers and regressions caught.

## 7. How to measure for real

- `app.getAppMetrics()` in main returns per-process type, PID, CPU, and memory. Log it on an interval, or expose it in the dev overlay (P7). This is the single most useful instrument; it shows exactly how much each browser process costs.
- macOS Activity Monitor, filter for the app: you will see one row per webview renderer process. Open desks with 1, then 5, then 10 browsers and watch the total.
- Chrome DevTools Performance panel on the renderer window during a pan/drag on a wire-dense desk shows the `LinkOverlay` and minimap costs directly.
- `chrome://tracing` style frame profiling confirms compositor jank on browser-heavy desks.

Replace the estimates in sections 2-4 with measured values once P7 exists.

---

### Key Findings:

1. **Browsers dominate memory usage** – Each browser is a full Chromium process that runs continuously, even when offscreen or hidden, leading to high RAM consumption and potential swap exhaustion.
2. **No viewport culling** – Every widget on the active desk is fully mounted and rendered, regardless of visibility, resulting in excessive memory and CPU load, especially on large desks.
3. **Live wires are a major CPU hot path** – During drag operations, `LinkOverlay` performs O(wires) DOM reads per frame, causing performance drops with 30+ wires.
4. **Minimap re-renders scale with widget count** – On dense desks, every layout change triggers a full re-render of all widgets as previews, adding significant CPU cost.
5. **Compositor jank on browser-heavy desks** – The lack of culling forces the compositor to manage many live webview layers, causing pan/zoom stutter.
6. **Non-browser widgets have a gentler cost curve**, but at high counts (e.g., >120), input latency and sluggishness become noticeable.

---

### Top 3 Recommendations:

1. **Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers** – Implement IntersectionObserver or visibility checks to pause or freeze browsers when fully off-screen, reducing memory and CPU load and preventing OS-level renderer kills.

2. **Viewport-cull the canvas** – Modify `Canvas.tsx` to skip mounting widgets outside the viewport (with margin), drastically reducing mount cost and improving pan/zoom performance—especially beneficial for browser-heavy desks.

3. **Soft-cap and warn on browser count per desk** – Track live webview count and provide a performance warning at ~8 browsers per desk to prevent unexpected instability without imposing hard limits.
